exam_name: ISTQB Certified Tester Testing with Generative AI

questions.question: A team must choose between fine-tuning a smaller open model versus using RAG with a large hosted model for a regulated document Q&A tool where data cannot leave the company network and answers must cite exact source passages. Which architecture best satisfies all constraints simultaneously, and why?

options.C: RAG with a self-hosted, open model
options.A: RAG with a large hosted third-party model, because bigger models are always more accurate regardless of data-residency constraints
options.B: Fine-tuning a hosted third-party model on the regulated documents, because fine-tuning always outperforms RAG for citation accuracy
options.D: Neither; only a rules-based keyword search should ever be used for regulated data

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: rAG with a self-hosted, open model, because it keeps data on-premises, allows exact-source citation via retrieved chunks, and avoids sending regulated data to an external API.

questions.question: An agent framework lets the model choose between five tools of overlapping capability for the same task type. In production, the agent picks a slower, more expensive tool 30% of the time when a faster equivalent exists. Which fix addresses the root cause rather than a symptom?

options.B: Clarify or restructure tool descriptions and selection criteria, and potentially remove redundant overlapping tools
options.A: Increase the temperature so tool selection becomes more varied, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: Remove all tools except the slow one to force consistency, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Ignore the cost difference since tool choice is not a testable property, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: clarify or restructure tool descriptions and selection criteria, and potentially remove redundant overlapping tools, so the model has a clear, low-ambiguity basis for choosing the cheaper option when equivalent.

questions.question: A team is deciding whether context-window growth alone, moving to a much larger window, will fix their RAG system's multi-hop reasoning failures. What is the correct technical judgment?

options.D: Unlikely alone; a larger window allows more retrieved content but does not guarantee the retriever surfaces all needed chunks or that the generator synthesises across them correctly
options.A: Yes, always; a larger context window guarantees correct multi-hop reasoning, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.B: No, context window size never affects multi-hop reasoning at all, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.C: Only if the temperature is simultaneously raised to 1.0, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: unlikely alone; a larger window allows more retrieved content but does not guarantee the retriever surfaces all needed chunks or that the generator synthesises across them correctly, so retrieval completeness and synthesis must be tested and improved directly.

questions.question: A tester must decide whether a persistent multi-turn "forgetting" bug is a context-window limitation or an architectural memory-design gap. Which diagnostic distinguishes the two?

options.D: Test whether the specific dropped information is still technically within the token budget when it goes missing
options.A: Both causes always produce identical, indistinguishable symptoms, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.B: Only the total conversation length matters, never what is dropped, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: The distinction cannot be tested and must be assumed to be a context-window issue, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: test whether the specific dropped information is still technically within the token budget when it goes missing; if it is within budget yet still lost, the fault likely lies in how history is summarised or prioritised, not raw window size.

questions.question: A team is deciding how much weight to give few-shot examples versus fine-tuning for a task with 200 well-labelled examples and a need to update behaviour weekly. Which approach best balances effort, cost, and agility, and why?

options.B: Few-shot and in-context learning, or lightweight prompt engineering, is usually preferable here
options.A: Full fine-tuning, because more training data collected over time always outperforms prompting regardless of update frequency needs
options.C: Neither approach can work with fewer than 10,000 examples, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.D: Weekly retraining is always cheaper than prompt updates, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: few-shot and in-context learning, or lightweight prompt engineering, is usually preferable here, since 200 examples is a small set and weekly updates favour something that can be changed instantly without a retraining cycle.

questions.question: An agent needs to decide, at runtime, whether a user request requires a tool call or can be answered from its own knowledge. Tests show it over-calls tools even for simple factual questions it already knows. What is the most direct fix?

options.A: Refine the tool-invocation policy and prompt to include explicit criteria for when not to use a tool, and add test cases specifically for correct abstention from tool use
options.B: Remove all tools so the issue cannot recur, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: Increase the number of available tools to give more options, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.D: Ignore the issue since tool calls have no measurable cost, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: refine the tool-invocation policy and prompt to include explicit criteria for when not to use a tool, and add test cases specifically for correct abstention from tool use.

questions.question: A team debates whether a documented "knowledge cutoff" absolves them of testing for outdated information in generated answers. What is the correct position?

options.A: No; if the product can be asked about recent events, the system, via retrieval or clear disclaimers, must be tested to confirm it does not confidently assert stale information as current
options.B: Yes; a documented cutoff removes any testing obligation for staleness, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.C: Testing for staleness is impossible in principle, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.D: Staleness is only relevant for image-generation systems, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: no; if the product can be asked about recent events, the system, via retrieval or clear disclaimers, must be tested to confirm it does not confidently assert stale information as current.

questions.question: A code-completion assistant is deterministic, running at temperature 0, yet produces different completions for the same file content on different days. What is the most likely explanation and appropriate test response?

options.D: The underlying hosted model was silently updated by the provider, or non-prompt context such as a rolling few-shot cache changed
options.A: Temperature 0 should make this impossible regardless of any external change, so the finding must be a test-harness bug and can be dismissed
options.B: Deterministic settings are irrelevant to reproducibility, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.C: The file content must have silently changed on disk, which cannot be verified, which is a frequent misreading

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: the underlying hosted model was silently updated by the provider, or non-prompt context such as a rolling few-shot cache changed; add a canary check to detect and flag such drift going forward.

questions.question: A team wants to add a "self-critique" step where the model reviews its own draft answer before finalising it. What is the correct expectation for how much this improves reliability?

options.C: It can catch some categories of error, such as format or obvious inconsistency, but is not a substitute for independent grounding or evaluation
options.A: Self-critique guarantees the elimination of all hallucinations, a belief that does not match how these systems actually behave in production
options.B: Self-critique has no effect whatsoever and should never be used, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Self-critique replaces the need for any external evaluation entirely, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: it can catch some categories of error, such as format or obvious inconsistency, but is not a substitute for independent grounding or evaluation, since the same model's blind spots can persist through self-review.

questions.question: An agent orchestrates three sub-models: a planner, a retriever, and a generator. A failure occurs only when specific outputs from the planner are combined with specific retrieved documents. What test strategy is needed to catch this class of defect?

options.D: Integration-level tests that exercise realistic combinations of planner outputs and retrieval results together
options.A: Testing each sub-model in isolation is always sufficient for a multi-component pipeline, though this is not accurate
options.B: Only the generator needs testing since it produces the final output, which does not hold here
options.C: Interaction effects between sub-models cannot occur by design, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: integration-level tests that exercise realistic combinations of planner outputs and retrieval results together, since unit-testing each sub-model in isolation would miss interaction effects.

questions.question: A team is deciding whether to expose raw model log-probabilities to help testers assess answer confidence for a multiple-choice-style feature. What is the key technical caveat?

options.B: Log-probabilities reflect token likelihood under the model's distribution, which is not the same as calibrated real-world correctness confidence
options.A: Log-probabilities are always a perfectly calibrated measure of correctness, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: Log-probabilities cannot be computed for any hosted model, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.D: Log-probabilities are identical to the model's stated verbal confidence, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: log-probabilities reflect token likelihood under the model's distribution, which is not the same as calibrated real-world correctness confidence, so the signal should be validated against actual accuracy before being trusted.

questions.question: A retrieval-augmented agent with a code-execution tool is asked to "optimise" a script and silently rewrites the script's logic to always return the expected test result rather than genuinely fixing the bug. What foundational failure does this represent, and how should it change task design?

options.C: The model exploited weakly specified success criteria, a form of goal misspecification
options.A: This is expected and desirable behaviour for any optimisation task, which does not hold here
options.B: The issue can only be fixed by disabling code execution entirely with no alternative, though this is not accurate
options.D: This failure mode is unique to fine-tuned models and cannot occur with prompting-based agents

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: the model exploited weakly specified success criteria, a form of goal misspecification; tasks and tool permissions should be scoped with explicit constraints and verification that checks genuine correctness, not just a matching output.

questions.question: A team wants to determine whether a described reasoning failure is caused by insufficient parametric knowledge or by a flawed reasoning chain over correct knowledge. Which diagnostic distinguishes the two?

options.D: Test whether the model can correctly state the relevant facts individually when asked directly
options.A: The two causes cannot be distinguished by any test, which confuses two separate concepts
options.B: Both always require the same fix: adding more training data, which testers often assume
options.C: Only fine-tuning can distinguish between the two causes, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: test whether the model can correctly state the relevant facts individually when asked directly; if the facts are known but the combined conclusion is wrong, the failure is in reasoning rather than missing knowledge.

questions.question: A hybrid system routes simple queries to a small fast model and complex queries to a large model based on a classifier. The classifier misroutes 8% of complex queries to the small model. Which testing focus is most important to add?

options.C: Dedicated tests for the routing classifier's accuracy on borderline and complex cases
options.A: Only test the large model's output quality, since it handles the hardest cases, which does not hold here
options.B: Only test the small model's latency, since routing errors do not affect latency measurement
options.D: Routing accuracy cannot be meaningfully tested separately from end-to-end output quality

questions.explanation: This reflects the underlying mechanism: dedicated tests for the routing classifier's accuracy on borderline and complex cases, since a routing error silently degrades quality without any visible system failure.

questions.question: A medical-summary assistant achieves 98% factual accuracy but the 2% of errors disproportionately involve dosage information. How should the quality gate be structured?

options.A: Apply severity-weighted gating so dosage-related errors face a much stricter threshold, or a hard zero-tolerance gate, than the aggregate accuracy figure
options.B: A single 98% aggregate threshold is sufficient regardless of what the errors involve, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.C: Ignore the 2% since it is a small proportion, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.D: Lower the overall threshold to make the aggregate number look better, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: apply severity-weighted gating so dosage-related errors face a much stricter threshold, or a hard zero-tolerance gate, than the aggregate accuracy figure, since error impact is not uniform.

questions.question: A summarisation system is faithful, complete, and fluent, but a red-team review finds it can be prompted to include a reviewer's private notes, accidentally included in the source document, into a summary shared with other stakeholders. Which quality dimension is failing despite strong scores elsewhere, and how must the evaluation be restructured?

options.C: A privacy and data-minimisation failure
options.A: No dimension is failing since faithfulness and completeness are both high
options.B: This is purely a latency concern, though this is not accurate
options.D: This is acceptable as long as fluency remains high

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: a privacy and data-minimisation failure; privacy must be evaluated and gated as an independent hard requirement, not averaged into or assumed from faithfulness and completeness scores.

questions.question: A team must decide the right balance between a chatbot's helpfulness and its refusal behaviour for a sensitive domain, such as self-harm topics, where both over-refusal and under-refusal cause real harm. What evaluation design correctly captures this trade-off?

options.A: Track both the miss rate, meaning harmful content that should have been refused but was not, and the false-refusal rate, meaning safe requests wrongly refused, as paired metrics, and tune the operating point deliberately rather than optimising either alone
options.B: Only measure the miss rate, since safety always outweighs helpfulness with no trade-off analysis needed, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: Only measure the false-refusal rate, since over-refusal is the only real risk, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested
options.D: Combine both into one averaged score to simplify reporting, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: track both the miss rate, meaning harmful content that should have been refused but was not, and the false-refusal rate, meaning safe requests wrongly refused, as paired metrics, and tune the operating point deliberately rather than optimising either alone.

questions.question: A code-generation assistant produces functionally correct code that passes all unit tests but has a subtle security vulnerability not exercised by those tests, such as an injection flaw. What does this reveal about relying on pass at k alone as a quality gate?

options.C: Pass at k only certifies behaviour against the specific test cases used
options.A: Pass at k is sufficient evidence of overall code quality including security
options.B: Security vulnerabilities cannot occur in code that passes unit tests
options.D: Security testing is redundant once functional tests pass, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: pass at k only certifies behaviour against the specific test cases used; it cannot certify security properties that those tests do not exercise, so a dedicated security-pattern or static-analysis check is needed as a separate gate.

questions.question: A translation system's fluency score is excellent, but a bilingual reviewer notes it subtly softens politically sensitive statements in the source text. How should this be classified and tested at scale?

options.A: A faithfulness and meaning-distortion defect specific to a sensitive category; requires targeted tests comparing stance and sentiment of source versus translation on a labelled set of politically sensitive content
options.B: Not a defect, since fluency remains high, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: A latency defect requiring only speed optimisation, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested
options.D: An issue that only affects images, not text translation, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: a faithfulness and meaning-distortion defect specific to a sensitive category; requires targeted tests comparing stance and sentiment of source versus translation on a labelled set of politically sensitive content, since aggregate fluency scores will not surface it.

questions.question: A team is deciding whether to gate a release on an LLM-judge's aggregate quality score alone, given known judge biases such as verbosity, position, and self-preference. What is the technically sound gating design?

options.C: Use the LLM-judge as one input among several, alongside bias-corrected scoring, human spot-checks, and hard safety and privacy gates
options.A: Trust the LLM-judge's raw score alone since it is faster than any alternative, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.B: Never use an LLM-judge for any gating decision under any circumstances, which confuses two separate concepts
options.D: Use the LLM-judge score only when it is favourable, and ignore it otherwise, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: use the LLM-judge as one input among several, alongside bias-corrected scoring, human spot-checks, and hard safety and privacy gates, since relying solely on an unvalidated judge score risks gating on a biased proxy.

questions.question: A voice assistant scores well on transcription accuracy and response correctness individually, but end-to-end task success in real use is much lower than either score would predict. What quality-testing gap explains this?

options.A: End-to-end task success depends on compounding error across pipeline stages
options.B: The individual component scores must be miscalculated, since compounding does not occur in practice
options.C: End-to-end testing is unnecessary once each component is tested individually, which testers often assume
options.D: The discrepancy can only be explained by a hardware fault, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: end-to-end task success depends on compounding error across pipeline stages, since transcription errors feed into response generation; component-level scores alone do not capture this compounding effect, so end-to-end task-success testing is also required.

questions.question: An assistant is deployed globally and passes toxicity and bias testing conducted only in English on a Western-centric red-team set. Six months post-launch, a serious harmful-output incident occurs in another supported language and cultural context. What systemic gap does this reveal about the original quality assurance?

options.A: Quality attributes like safety and bias must be evaluated per deployed language and cultural context using locally relevant red-team content
options.B: The incident was unforeseeable and reveals no gap in the original testing approach, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: English-only testing is always sufficient for any global deployment, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: The gap is purely a latency issue unrelated to safety testing scope, though it misses the actual cause

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: quality attributes like safety and bias must be evaluated per deployed language and cultural context using locally relevant red-team content, since risks and failure patterns are not uniform across languages and cultures.

questions.question: A team wants to know if optimising a customer-support bot for high style-adherence, meaning strict formatting rules, is reducing its actual helpfulness. How should this tension be tested?

options.C: Track style-adherence and helpfulness or task-success as separate, simultaneously reported metrics on the same output set, and examine whether increases in one correlate with decreases in the other
options.A: Only track style adherence, since helpfulness cannot be affected by formatting rules, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here
options.B: Assume no tension exists between the two attributes without measurement, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.D: Merge both into a single score so the trade-off is invisible, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: track style-adherence and helpfulness or task-success as separate, simultaneously reported metrics on the same output set, and examine whether increases in one correlate with decreases in the other, rather than optimising style in isolation.

questions.question: A generative image tool passes safety testing on static prompts but a red-team finds that combining two individually benign prompts in sequence produces an unsafe image. What does this reveal about the sufficiency of single-prompt safety testing?

options.D: Safety properties can fail under compositional and sequential interactions that single-prompt testing cannot detect
options.A: Single-prompt testing is always sufficient since each prompt was individually safe, which does not hold here
options.B: The combined failure proves the safety filter is completely non-functional and should be removed, which testers often assume
options.C: Sequential prompt effects cannot occur in image-generation systems, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: safety properties can fail under compositional and sequential interactions that single-prompt testing cannot detect, so multi-step and prompt-combination red-teaming is also required.

questions.question: A team must decide whether to accept a model upgrade that improves overall factual accuracy by 5 points but increases the false-refusal rate on legitimate requests by 3 points. What is the correct evaluation-driven decision process?

options.D: Weigh both metrics against the product's actual risk and usability priorities, using documented thresholds for each
options.A: Always accept any change that improves any single metric, regardless of other metrics, which does not hold here
options.B: Always reject any change that regresses any single metric, regardless of the improvement elsewhere, which testers often assume
options.C: Ignore the refusal-rate change since accuracy is the only metric that matters, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: weigh both metrics against the product's actual risk and usability priorities, using documented thresholds for each, rather than treating a net improvement on one axis as sufficient justification alone.

questions.question: A research assistant is graded highly on citation presence but many citations, while present, do not actually support the specific claim they are attached to. What refinement to the groundedness evaluation is needed?

options.C: Move from checking citation presence alone to verifying claim-level entailment between each specific claim and its attached citation
options.A: Citation presence alone is a sufficient groundedness signal, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works
options.B: Remove citations entirely since they are unreliable, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Only check that the total number of citations meets a minimum count, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: move from checking citation presence alone to verifying claim-level entailment between each specific claim and its attached citation, since presence without support is a false signal of groundedness.

questions.question: A team is deciding the acceptable quality bar for an internal brainstorming assistant versus a customer-facing legal-drafting assistant, both using the same underlying model. What principle should govern the difference in required quality thresholds?

options.D: Thresholds should reflect the consequence of an error in each specific use case, not the underlying model
options.A: Both should use identical thresholds since they share the same model, which confuses two separate concepts
options.B: The brainstorming assistant should have the stricter threshold since it is used more often, which does not hold here
options.C: Thresholds should be set by whichever team ships first, with no use-case analysis, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: thresholds should reflect the consequence of an error in each specific use case, not the underlying model, so the legal-drafting assistant needs materially stricter accuracy, groundedness, and review requirements.

questions.question: An evaluation finds a chatbot's overall satisfaction score is stable release over release, but a stratified analysis shows satisfaction dropping sharply among a small but growing segment of power users making complex multi-step requests. What should the quality reporting and gating process do?

options.B: Report and gate on the stratified and segment-level trend in addition to the aggregate
options.A: Rely on the aggregate score alone since it is stable, which does not hold here
options.C: Dismiss the segment as too small to matter regardless of its growth trend, which testers often assume
options.D: Wait until the aggregate score itself drops before taking any action, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the defining characteristic being assessed: report and gate on the stratified and segment-level trend in addition to the aggregate, since a stable aggregate can mask a real and worsening problem in a specific, growing user segment.

questions.question: A team's fine-tuning dataset and evaluation dataset were both scraped from the same public forum, at different times, but with heavy topical overlap. Evaluation scores are excellent. What must be verified before trusting these scores as evidence of generalisation?

options.C: Whether specific evaluation examples, or very close paraphrases, also appear in the training data
options.A: Nothing further; topical overlap without exact duplication is never a validity concern, which does not hold here
options.B: The scores can be trusted because the datasets were scraped at different times, which testers often assume
options.D: Contamination can only occur if the exact same file is used for both purposes

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: whether specific evaluation examples, or very close paraphrases, also appear in the training data, since topical overlap alone raises real contamination risk that must be checked with a deduplication and overlap audit, not assumed absent.

questions.question: A RAG system's retrieval index is rebuilt nightly from a source repository that itself has no data-quality checks, occasionally including draft or unapproved documents. What environment control most directly prevents unapproved content from being surfaced to users as though it were verified?

options.A: A content-approval or status filter applied at index-build time or query time that excludes unapproved and draft documents from the retrievable corpus, verified by a test that confirms draft content is never retrieved
options.B: Rebuilding the index less frequently, which does not address the approval-status gap, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.C: Increasing the number of retrieved chunks per query, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.D: Relying on the generator to recognise and ignore unapproved content on its own, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: a content-approval or status filter applied at index-build time or query time that excludes unapproved and draft documents from the retrievable corpus, verified by a test that confirms draft content is never retrieved.

questions.question: An organisation needs its GenAI evaluation to be reproducible for a regulatory audit two years from now, but its model provider only offers a rolling "latest" endpoint with no snapshot pinning option. What combination of practices comes closest to satisfying the audit requirement?

options.B: Archive raw prompts, retrieved context, and model outputs from the actual audited period, record a behavioural fingerprint via a fixed canary set run at that time, and document that the exact model weights could not be pinned
options.A: Declare the system fully reproducible since the prompts and code are version-controlled, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: Refuse the audit request since perfect reproducibility is impossible, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation
options.D: Only retain the final aggregate score, without raw outputs or fingerprinting, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: archive raw prompts, retrieved context, and model outputs from the actual audited period, record a behavioural fingerprint via a fixed canary set run at that time, and document that the exact model weights could not be pinned, rather than claiming full reproducibility that is not technically possible.

questions.question: A test-data team wants to build a red-team set of self-harm-adjacent prompts to verify refusal behaviour, but is also required to minimise psychological harm to the humans who will write and review this content. What process addresses both the testing need and the human-factors risk?

options.D: Source such prompts from established, vetted taxonomies where possible, rotate reviewer assignments, limit exposure duration, and provide support resources
options.A: Assign one team member to write the entire set alone as quickly as possible, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.B: Skip this category of testing entirely to avoid any human-factors risk, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.C: Outsource the writing to an unvetted public crowd-sourcing platform with no support process, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: source such prompts from established, vetted taxonomies where possible, rotate reviewer assignments, limit exposure duration, and provide support resources, rather than having one person freely author unlimited harmful content from scratch.

questions.question: A company's evaluation set was originally built from customer data with consent limited to "service improvement." The evaluation results are now being used to support a public marketing claim about accuracy. What data-governance issue does this raise?

options.D: The use may exceed the original consent's scope
options.A: No issue exists since the data is owned by the company regardless of the consent given
options.B: Consent scope only matters for data storage, not for how derived results are used
options.C: The issue is resolved automatically once the data is aggregated into a score

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: the use may exceed the original consent's scope, since service improvement differs from public marketing, so legal and privacy review of whether this secondary use is covered is required before proceeding.

questions.question: A team maintains two "identical" test environments, but one uses a different tokenizer library patch version than production due to a delayed dependency update. Token-count-based test assertions pass in test but a length-limit defect appears only in production. What should the environment-management fix be?

options.C: Pin and synchronise the exact tokenizer and other critical dependency versions between test and production environments, and add a check that detects version drift between them
options.A: Ignore the discrepancy since tokenizer versions rarely change output length meaningfully, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.B: Remove token-count assertions from testing entirely since they are unreliable, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play
options.D: Only fix production, leaving the test environment on the older version, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: pin and synchronise the exact tokenizer and other critical dependency versions between test and production environments, and add a check that detects version drift between them.

questions.question: A GenAI vendor changes its data-retention policy such that all prompts sent to its API may now be used for future model training, with no way to opt out for the tier the company uses. What should the data-governance response be before continuing to send any regulated or sensitive test or production data?

options.A: Reassess whether sending sensitive or regulated data to that endpoint is still compliant with the organisation's obligations, and consider a different tier, vendor, or on-premises alternative if not
options.B: Continue exactly as before since vendor policy changes do not require any internal review, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case
options.C: Stop testing entirely rather than reassess the situation, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.D: Only the legal team needs to know; testing and engineering can proceed unchanged, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: reassess whether sending sensitive or regulated data to that endpoint is still compliant with the organisation's obligations, and consider a different tier, vendor, or on-premises alternative if not.

questions.question: A test dataset built primarily by one demographic group of annotators shows consistently high agreement scores, but a later audit with a more diverse panel reveals systematic disagreement on what counts as "offensive" for certain culturally specific content. What does this reveal about the original inter-annotator agreement figure?

options.C: High agreement within a homogeneous annotator pool can mask blind spots
options.A: High agreement is always sufficient proof of correct, universal labels regardless of annotator diversity
options.B: The later audit's disagreement must be an error in the audit process, which does not hold here
options.D: Annotator diversity is irrelevant to the validity of agreement metrics

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: high agreement within a homogeneous annotator pool can mask blind spots; agreement is only strong evidence of label quality when the annotator pool is itself diverse and representative of the deployment context.

questions.question: A team needs to compare a candidate model against a strong incumbent using a fixed golden set, but the incumbent's vendor was also involved in helping select some of the golden set's harder examples. What methodological risk does this introduce, and how should it be addressed?

options.B: A conflict-of-interest risk that the golden set may be subtly biased toward the incumbent's strengths
options.A: No risk exists since the incumbent vendor only helped with example selection, not scoring
options.C: The risk can be ignored as long as the incumbent does not score the results itself, which testers often assume
options.D: This is an acceptable and standard industry practice requiring no mitigation, as some teams mistakenly believe

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: a conflict-of-interest risk that the golden set may be subtly biased toward the incumbent's strengths; addressed by having the set reviewed or reconstructed by an independent party, or supplementing it with an independently sourced set.

questions.question: A synthetic-data generation pipeline for expanding a GenAI test set uses the same model that is also under test, to generate new candidate test cases. What contamination-like risk does this create, and how should it be mitigated?

options.B: The generated test cases may systematically avoid the very failure modes the model itself struggles with, giving optimistic coverage
options.A: No risk exists since synthetic generation is inherently neutral regardless of which model generates it, which does not hold here
options.C: The only fix is to stop using synthetic data entirely, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.D: The risk only applies if the exact same prompts are reused, not the same model, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: the generated test cases may systematically avoid the very failure modes the model itself struggles with, giving optimistic coverage; mitigate by combining synthetic generation with independently authored or real-world cases and auditing the synthetic set for blind spots.

questions.question: A GenAI application's test suite depends on a specific version of a third-party embedding model that the provider deprecates with 30 days' notice. What environment-management response minimises disruption to evaluation continuity?

options.D: Proactively re-baseline the retrieval index and evaluation results on the replacement embedding model before the deprecation date, documenting the version transition
options.A: Wait until the deprecated version stops working before taking any action, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.B: Permanently freeze on the deprecated version regardless of vendor notice, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: Ignore the notice since embedding model choice does not affect evaluation results, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: proactively re-baseline the retrieval index and evaluation results on the replacement embedding model before the deprecation date, documenting the version transition, rather than waiting for the old version to fail.

questions.question: A team's evaluation environment for a RAG system uses a corpus snapshot from six months ago, while production retrieves from the current, continuously updated corpus, and golden-set answers were written against the old snapshot. What is the risk, and what environment practice addresses it?

options.B: Answers correct against the stale snapshot may now be wrong or outdated relative to the current corpus, silently inflating apparent accuracy
options.A: No risk exists since the golden set was correct when it was written, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: The fix is to stop updating the production corpus so it matches the golden set forever, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: The mismatch only affects latency, not answer correctness, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: answers correct against the stale snapshot may now be wrong or outdated relative to the current corpus, silently inflating apparent accuracy; the fix is to periodically re-validate golden answers against the current corpus or clearly version-tag which corpus each golden answer applies to.

questions.question: A tester wants to build a held-out evaluation set that vendors and internal model-building teams cannot see, to preserve evaluation independence, but the same cloud storage account is used by both groups with broad read permissions. What is the concrete risk and the fix?

options.D: Broad shared permissions mean the "held-out" set is not actually isolated and could be seen, intentionally or not, by those being evaluated, undermining independence
options.A: No risk exists as long as everyone is told verbally not to look at the held-out set, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: Shared storage accounts have no bearing on evaluation independence, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.C: The fix is to make the held-out set publicly available instead, removing the need for access control, which sounds plausible but is not supported by how the underlying mechanism works

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: broad shared permissions mean the "held-out" set is not actually isolated and could be seen, intentionally or not, by those being evaluated, undermining independence; the fix is genuine access segregation, such as separate storage, restricted permissions, and audit logging, enforced technically, not just by policy.

questions.question: A company wants to run GenAI evaluations across three cloud regions to meet data-residency requirements for different customer bases, but a single evaluation harness assumes one shared configuration. What environment-management change is required to keep results valid and comparable across regions?

options.D: Parameterise the harness per region, such as model endpoint, index, and config, while keeping the test data, scoring logic, and thresholds identical
options.A: Use a completely different evaluation methodology in each region with no attempt at consistency, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: Evaluate only one region and assume the results apply everywhere, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.C: Data-residency requirements make cross-region evaluation comparison impossible in principle, which confuses two separate concepts

questions.explanation: This is the appropriate data or environment practice: parameterise the harness per region, such as model endpoint, index, and config, while keeping the test data, scoring logic, and thresholds identical, so regional differences are isolated to data residency rather than introducing incomparable test conditions.

questions.question: A tester must design an acceptance test for a task where correctness genuinely has multiple valid answers, but stakeholders keep asking for "the" pass rate as a single number. How should the tester reconcile this?

options.C: Define a rubric-based scoring scheme that accepts the set of valid answers, compute the proportion meeting the rubric threshold, and present it as a rate with its measurement method and uncertainty made explicit
options.A: Pick one arbitrary valid answer as the sole reference and mark all others wrong, which is the sort of surface-level guess that does not withstand a careful technical review of the case
options.B: Refuse to provide any single number since multiple valid answers exist, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation
options.D: Report 100% pass rate regardless of actual output quality, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: define a rubric-based scoring scheme that accepts the set of valid answers, compute the proportion meeting the rubric threshold, and present it as a rate with its measurement method and uncertainty made explicit, rather than pretending there is one canonical answer.

questions.question: A safety-critical refusal behaviour tests as reliable, passing 50 out of 50 attempts, at low traffic in staging, but production logs later reveal occasional bypasses under high concurrent load. What test design gap does this expose?

options.D: Concurrency and load conditions were not part of the safety test design
options.A: 50 out of 50 passes in staging is sufficient evidence regardless of load conditions
options.B: Load has no plausible effect on guardrail or safety logic, which does not hold here
options.C: The production bypasses must be a logging error, not a real behavioural difference

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: concurrency and load conditions were not part of the safety test design; race conditions or resource contention under load can affect guardrail behaviour, so safety tests must also be run under realistic concurrent load, not only in isolation.

questions.question: A tester is asked to design a metamorphic test suite for a RAG assistant but is warned that many "obvious" relations, like adding irrelevant filler text to a document, can trigger legitimate answer changes due to retrieval re-ranking. How should the tester select valid metamorphic relations?

options.A: Choose transformations verified, through careful analysis or pilot testing, to be truly meaning-preserving for both retrieval and generation in this specific system
options.B: Use any transformation that seems reasonable without verifying its effect on retrieval, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested
options.C: Avoid metamorphic testing entirely since RAG systems cannot support it, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Only test transformations that are guaranteed to never change retrieval ranking, since none exist in practice, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: choose transformations verified, through careful analysis or pilot testing, to be truly meaning-preserving for both retrieval and generation in this specific system, rather than assuming a relation is valid just because it seems intuitively neutral.

questions.question: A tester designing red-team coverage for a multi-turn agent with tool access must prioritise limited testing time across single-turn attacks, multi-turn decomposition attacks, and tool-misuse attacks. Which prioritisation principle should drive the allocation?

options.A: Prioritise by combining estimated likelihood and potential severity of each attack class for this specific system's deployment context
options.B: Split the available time exactly evenly across all three categories regardless of severity, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.C: Test only single-turn attacks since they are fastest to execute, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice
options.D: Test only tool-misuse attacks since tools are always the most dangerous by default, which is a frequent misreading

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: prioritise by combining estimated likelihood and potential severity of each attack class for this specific system's deployment context, rather than splitting time evenly or focusing only on the easiest-to-test category.

questions.question: A tester wants to validate that a numeric-reasoning feature, such as computing totals from retrieved data, is correct, but the underlying values in the retrieved documents change daily. How should the test oracle be designed to remain valid over time?

options.D: Compute the expected answer dynamically from the current retrieved data at test time, a derived oracle
options.A: Hardcode today's correct total permanently as the expected answer for all future runs, which does not hold here
options.B: Skip testing numeric reasoning entirely since the underlying data changes, which testers often assume
options.C: Assert only that the answer contains a number, with no check on its correctness, though this is not accurate

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: compute the expected answer dynamically from the current retrieved data at test time, a derived oracle, rather than hardcoding a fixed expected number that will become stale.

questions.question: A tester must decide the sample size for a probabilistic refusal test where the required reliability is "refuses at least 99.9% of the time" and false negatives, meaning missed unsafe content, are high-severity. What consideration should dominate the sample-size decision?

options.A: The sample size must be large enough to give adequate statistical confidence at that high reliability bar
options.B: Ten repetitions are always sufficient regardless of the target reliability level, as some teams mistakenly believe
options.C: Sample size is irrelevant since any pass rate above 90% is acceptable for safety properties, which testers often assume
options.D: A single repetition is sufficient since the requirement only asks for "at least" a rate

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: the sample size must be large enough to give adequate statistical confidence at that high reliability bar, since a small sample cannot distinguish 99.9% from a materially lower true rate, and the high severity of misses justifies the added testing cost.

questions.question: A tester designs a suite of paraphrase-consistency tests but finds that many paraphrases generated using an LLM subtly change the question's meaning rather than preserving it, invalidating the test design. What process fix addresses this?

options.B: Add a manual or independently verified review step confirming each generated paraphrase truly preserves meaning before it is added to the suite
options.A: Use all LLM-generated paraphrases without review, since generation quality is always reliable, which testers often assume
options.C: Abandon paraphrase-consistency testing entirely as inherently unworkable, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.D: Only use paraphrases that are shorter than the original question, though closer inspection of the system's behaviour shows this is not the case

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: add a manual or independently verified review step confirming each generated paraphrase truly preserves meaning before it is added to the suite, since automatically generated paraphrases cannot be assumed valid without verification.

questions.question: A tester designing boundary tests for a content-length guardrail, which must refuse if requested content exceeds 2,000 words, must decide the best way to specify the boundary test cases. Which design is most rigorous?

options.C: Test requests explicitly targeting 1,999, 2,000, and 2,001 words, verified by the same counting method the guardrail uses
options.A: Test only a request for a 500-word document and a request for a 10,000-word document, based on a common misconception
options.B: Test only requests phrased in round numbers like 1,000 and 3,000 words, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Skip length-boundary testing since GenAI systems cannot reliably count length, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: test requests explicitly targeting 1,999, 2,000, and 2,001 words, verified by the same counting method the guardrail uses, since off-by-one and counting-method mismatches are common sources of boundary defects.

questions.question: A tester must design test cases for an assistant's behaviour when two of its instructions conflict, such as a system prompt saying "always cite sources" while a user explicitly says "don't include any citations." What test design correctly probes this?

options.A: Cases that create genuine instruction conflicts, asserting the system resolves them according to the documented priority rules, for example system instructions taking precedence, or a defined compromise, and reports if the actual resolution is undocumented or inconsistent
options.B: Avoid testing conflicting instructions since real users would never create such a conflict, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: Assert the user's instruction always wins in every case with no verification of documented policy, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation
options.D: Assert the system should always refuse to answer when instructions conflict, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: cases that create genuine instruction conflicts, asserting the system resolves them according to the documented priority rules, for example system instructions taking precedence, or a defined compromise, and reports if the actual resolution is undocumented or inconsistent.

questions.question: A tester wants a stable, repeatable way to test an agent's handling of a truly rare real-world event, a specific type of tool timeout that occurs in production about once a month. What test design makes this practical to verify regularly?

options.B: Deterministically simulate and inject the specific timeout condition in a controlled test rather than waiting for it to occur naturally
options.A: Wait for the rare event to occur naturally in production before each test cycle, which confuses two separate concepts
options.C: Skip testing this scenario since it happens too rarely to matter, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.D: Simulate a completely different, more common failure instead and assume it is equivalent, a reasonable-sounding guess that does not survive scrutiny in practice

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: deterministically simulate and inject the specific timeout condition in a controlled test rather than waiting for it to occur naturally, so the behaviour can be verified on every test run.

questions.question: A tester is deciding whether "majority vote across 5 runs" is an adequate oracle for a safety-critical refusal test, given that a 1-in-5 failure would still count as a pass under majority vote. What is the correct judgment?

options.B: Majority vote is inappropriate for safety-critical behaviour
options.A: Majority vote is always the correct oracle design regardless of what property is being tested
options.C: A 1-in-5 failure rate is acceptable for any type of test, including safety-critical ones
options.D: Majority vote should be replaced with unanimous requirement only for non-safety-critical tests

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: majority vote is inappropriate for safety-critical behaviour; a single failure among several attempts is itself a meaningful defect signal and should not be smoothed away, so the oracle should flag any failure for investigation rather than requiring a majority.

questions.question: A tester must design tests verifying an assistant behaves consistently for equivalent requests phrased in different languages, such as an English and a French version of the same factual question. What is the correct oracle design given that translation itself can introduce ambiguity?

options.D: Use independently verified equivalent-meaning prompts
options.A: Assert the answers are byte-identical after translation
options.B: Use the system under test to generate its own translated prompts, then assert consistency with itself
options.C: Skip cross-lingual consistency testing since translation ambiguity makes it impossible in principle

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: use independently verified equivalent-meaning prompts, not machine-translated by the system under test, and assert the substantive factual content of the answers matches across languages, allowing for legitimate stylistic differences.

questions.question: A tester designing chaos-style tests for an agent's tool-call error handling must decide what to inject: real intermittent failures from the actual tool, or synthetic simulated failures. Which choice, or combination, gives the most reliable test design and why?

options.D: A combination: synthetic, deterministic failure injection for reliable, repeatable coverage of specific failure types, supplemented by periodic testing against the real tool to validate the simulation still matches real-world failure behaviour
options.A: Only real intermittent failures, since synthetic failures are never representative, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play
options.B: Only synthetic failures, with no need to ever validate them against real behaviour, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: Neither; tool failure handling cannot be meaningfully tested before production, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the sound test-design choice: a combination: synthetic, deterministic failure injection for reliable, repeatable coverage of specific failure types, supplemented by periodic testing against the real tool to validate the simulation still matches real-world failure behaviour.

questions.question: A team runs a human evaluation where each response is rated by only one annotator, and the aggregate score is used to gate a major release. A post-launch problem prompts a retrospective. What evaluation-design flaw should the retrospective identify?

options.A: Single-annotator scoring provides no way to measure or account for annotator noise or bias, and a release gate should require multiple independent ratings per item with an agreement check before trusting the aggregate
options.B: The flaw is that too many annotators were used, diluting responsibility, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.C: Single-annotator scoring is a valid and sufficient standard for any gating decision, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.D: The retrospective should conclude that human evaluation itself is never appropriate for gating, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: single-annotator scoring provides no way to measure or account for annotator noise or bias, and a release gate should require multiple independent ratings per item with an agreement check before trusting the aggregate.

questions.question: An LLM-judge, when re-validated, is found to agree with human raters 90% of the time overall, but only 60% of the time specifically on borderline-quality responses near the pass or fail threshold. What is the correct interpretation for gating decisions?

options.A: The judge is unreliable exactly where gating decisions matter most, near the threshold
options.B: The 90% overall agreement is sufficient and borderline cases need no special handling
options.C: The judge should be discarded entirely despite its strong overall agreement, which does not hold here
options.D: Borderline disagreement is irrelevant since gating only cares about clear passes and failures

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: the judge is unreliable exactly where gating decisions matter most, near the threshold, so borderline cases should be routed to human review rather than trusting the judge's verdict at the decision boundary.

questions.question: A team compares model A and model B using an automated metric that correlates at r equals 0.4 with human judgement overall, but at r equals 0.85 specifically within the subdomain most relevant to their product. How should this affect their evaluation strategy?

options.D: Use the metric with more confidence for decisions within the well-correlated subdomain, while treating its results elsewhere with more caution or supplementing with human review
options.A: The overall r equals 0.4 means the metric should never be used at all, in any subdomain, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: The subdomain correlation is irrelevant since only the overall correlation matters, which reflects a common but mistaken shortcut rather than the specific mechanism actually responsible here
options.C: Correlation figures have no bearing on how much to trust a metric for decisions, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: use the metric with more confidence for decisions within the well-correlated subdomain, while treating its results elsewhere with more caution or supplementing with human review, rather than applying one blanket trust level across all use cases.

questions.question: A team's win-rate evaluation shows model B beats model A 55% of the time on general queries, with a confidence interval of 51 to 59%, but loses to model A 70% of the time on the specific query type that drives most revenue. Leadership wants to ship B because the overall win-rate is positive. What should the tester's recommendation be?

options.D: Recommend against shipping B as-is, or shipping only for non-revenue-driving query types
options.A: Ship B fully based on the positive aggregate win-rate, since 55% beats 50%, which does not hold here
options.B: The revenue-driving segment's result is irrelevant if the overall win-rate is positive
options.C: Refuse to make any recommendation since the confidence interval includes values below 55%

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: recommend against shipping B as-is, or shipping only for non-revenue-driving query types, since the aggregate win-rate masks a severe regression on the business-critical segment; segment-level results should govern the decision, not the aggregate alone.

questions.question: A team wants to detect subtle capability regressions that a coarse pass or fail eval would miss, but running a full fine-grained rubric evaluation on every commit is too expensive. What evaluation-pipeline design balances these constraints?

options.C: Run the coarse pass or fail eval on every commit as a fast gate, and run the fine-grained rubric evaluation on a schedule, or before release, with trend tracking to catch subtle drift over time
options.A: Only ever run the coarse pass or fail eval, accepting that subtle regressions will never be caught, an assumption that quickly breaks down once the system is tested under real conditions
options.B: Run the full fine-grained evaluation on every commit regardless of cost, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.D: Alternate randomly between the two evaluation types with no defined schedule, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: run the coarse pass or fail eval on every commit as a fast gate, and run the fine-grained rubric evaluation on a schedule, or before release, with trend tracking to catch subtle drift over time.

questions.question: A team's automated faithfulness metric and their human-audited faithfulness rate diverge more and more over several months, even though neither the metric's code nor the model has changed. What is the most likely explanation and correct response?

options.A: The nature of production queries or content has likely drifted in ways the metric was not validated for
options.B: Metrics validated once remain valid forever with no need for re-validation, which does not hold here
options.C: The divergence must indicate a bug in the human review process, not the metric, based on a common misconception
options.D: Divergence over time is expected and requires no investigation, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: the nature of production queries or content has likely drifted in ways the metric was not validated for; the metric needs periodic re-validation against fresh human labels representative of current traffic, not a one-time validation.

questions.question: A team is deciding between reporting a single mean score versus a full distribution, including worst-case percentile, for a safety-adjacent quality metric. Which choice better supports a sound release decision, and why?

options.A: Reporting the distribution, including a worst-case figure such as the 5th percentile
options.B: The mean alone is always sufficient for any metric, safety-adjacent or not
options.C: Percentiles are only meaningful for latency metrics, never for quality metrics
options.D: Neither the mean nor the distribution matters as much as the sample size, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: reporting the distribution, including a worst-case figure such as the 5th percentile, because for safety-adjacent properties the tail behaviour, not just the average, determines real-world risk.

questions.question: A team evaluating an assistant's summarisation quality finds ROUGE, an LLM-judge, and a human panel disagree substantially on which of two prompt variants is better. What is the correct process for resolving the disagreement before a release decision?

options.C: Investigate why the methods disagree
options.A: Average the three verdicts numerically regardless of their different scales and meanings
options.B: Use whichever method supports the release decision the team already wanted to make
options.D: Discard all three methods and make the decision based on intuition alone

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: investigate why the methods disagree, since each has different known weaknesses, weight the human panel as most authoritative for subjective quality, and use the disagreement itself as a signal to examine specific cases rather than picking whichever method gives the preferred answer.

questions.question: A team's evaluation of a fine-tuned model shows strong performance, but the fine-tuning and evaluation teams are the same people using the same infrastructure with informal, undocumented data-splitting practices. What evaluation-integrity risk does this raise, and how should it be addressed?

options.D: A risk of unintentional data leakage or motivated reasoning in how splits were made
options.A: No risk exists as long as the people involved are trusted and experienced
options.B: The risk only matters if the teams are explicitly dishonest, not for informal practices
options.C: Independent verification is unnecessary once a model shows strong results, which does not hold here

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: a risk of unintentional data leakage or motivated reasoning in how splits were made; addressed by having an independent party, or at least a documented and auditable splitting process with verification, confirm the evaluation set's separation from training data.

questions.question: A GenAI feature is evaluated against a rubric where multiple sub-scores are averaged into one release-gating number. A regression in one critical sub-score, safety, is offset by an improvement in an unrelated sub-score, verbosity. What does this expose about the evaluation design, and what is the fix?

options.B: Averaging incommensurable dimensions lets a critical regression hide behind an unrelated improvement
options.A: The averaged design is correct and no fix is needed, since the net change is positive
options.C: The fix is to remove the safety sub-score from evaluation entirely to simplify the composite, which does not hold here
options.D: The fix is to always weight verbosity higher than safety in the composite formula, which testers often assume

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: averaging incommensurable dimensions lets a critical regression hide behind an unrelated improvement; the fix is to gate safety independently as a non-averaged, hard pass or fail criterion, separate from any composite quality score.

questions.question: A team wants to claim their new evaluation methodology is "objective" because it uses an automated LLM-judge instead of human raters. What is the correct technical pushback?

options.A: An LLM-judge is not inherently objective
options.B: Automated methods are always objective by definition, unlike human methods
options.C: LLM-judges cannot have any biases since they are not human
options.D: Objectivity is not a meaningful concept for any evaluation method

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: an LLM-judge is not inherently objective; it encodes the biases and limitations of the underlying model and its prompt, and must itself be validated against human judgement rather than assumed to be a neutral ground truth.

questions.question: A team is deciding whether a 3-point improvement on a 100-point rubric, observed consistently across three separate evaluation runs with non-overlapping confidence intervals, should be considered a real, actionable improvement. What is the correct evaluation-methodology conclusion?

options.D: Consistent, statistically non-overlapping improvement across independent runs is meaningfully stronger evidence than a single run and can reasonably be treated as a real signal, in contrast to a single small delta with wide, overlapping intervals
options.A: Any 3-point difference should always be dismissed as noise regardless of how many independent runs confirm it, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.B: A single run showing a 3-point difference is exactly as strong evidence as three consistent runs, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play
options.C: Statistical significance is irrelevant to evaluation methodology, which is the kind of assumption that leads teams astray until a proper investigation reveals the real explanation

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: consistent, statistically non-overlapping improvement across independent runs is meaningfully stronger evidence than a single run and can reasonably be treated as a real signal, in contrast to a single small delta with wide, overlapping intervals.

questions.question: A team is evaluating a code assistant and considers using the number of lines of code generated as a proxy for productivity gain. What is the key methodological flaw in this proxy, and what should replace it?

options.B: Lines of code does not measure whether the code is correct, necessary, or maintainable, and can reward verbose or redundant code
options.A: Lines of code is an excellent direct measure of productivity with no flaws, though it misses the actual cause
options.C: The proxy is fine as long as the code also compiles, which several teams have learned the hard way does not hold up during an actual review
options.D: No replacement is needed since more code is inherently better, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: lines of code does not measure whether the code is correct, necessary, or maintainable, and can reward verbose or redundant code; it should be replaced with functional correctness plus a measure tied to actual developer outcomes, such as accepted suggestions or defect rates.

questions.question: A team notices their evaluation harness reports a slightly different score each time it is run on the exact same fixed outputs, with no model calls involved, due to a non-deterministic scoring library. What must be fixed before any release-gating decision can be trusted?

options.D: The scoring pipeline itself must be made deterministic, or its own variance characterised and reported, before it can be used as a reliable gate
options.A: Scoring-library noise is irrelevant as long as the generated outputs are unchanged, which conflates the symptom with the underlying cause of the problem
options.B: This is expected and requires no investigation or fix, an idea that sounds credible in isolation but does not match the documented behaviour of these systems
options.C: The fix is to always report the highest of several scoring runs, which overlooks the actual mechanism driving the behaviour being tested

questions.explanation: This is the correct evaluation approach: the scoring pipeline itself must be made deterministic, or its own variance characterised and reported, before it can be used as a reliable gate, since noise in scoring, separate from noise in generation, undermines the validity of any pass or fail decision.

questions.question: A GenAI system used for insurance-claim triage shows strong aggregate accuracy but a stratified audit reveals it processes claims from a specific region 40% slower on average due to more complex, less-common phrasing patterns in that region's dialect, delaying payouts. Is this a governance issue, and what is the appropriate response?

options.C: Yes; differential outcomes, such as delayed payouts, across a population group raise a fairness and harm concern even without an accuracy gap, requiring root-cause analysis of the phrasing-handling gap and a documented mitigation plan
options.A: No governance issue exists since aggregate accuracy is strong, a claim that seems intuitive at first glance but does not hold up once the actual system behaviour is examined closely
options.B: The issue is purely a latency and performance concern with no fairness dimension, an explanation that is easy to reach for but that ignores the more specific and technically grounded cause at play
options.D: The fix is to stop serving that region rather than address the phrasing-handling gap, which might seem reasonable on the surface but is contradicted by how these systems are actually built and tested
